title: Kudzu: The Vine That Just Won't Stop
summary: Hosts explore kudzu, the invasive vine from Asia that has become a symbol of the American South. They cover its growth habits and massive taproots, its traditional use as food and medicine in China and Japan, the false story of its 1876 Philadelphia Centennial debut, and its ornamental spread. They explain how the 1930s government soil-erosion program promoted planting it, how evangelist Channing Cope boosted it, and how it later overran farms. They cover its federal noxious-weed listing, biodiversity and nitrogen concerns, questions about how overblown kudzu statistics are, the kudzu bug stink bug, and removal methods. They close with the Brooklyn Nine-Nine listener mail and a James Dickey poem about kudzu.

segments.title: Opening and kudzu introduction
segments.summary: Hosts introduce kudzu as a Japanese or Chinese invasive vine that has come to symbolize the American South, and note its scientific name Pueraria montana.

segments.title: Kudzu growth and habits
segments.summary: The hosts describe kudzu as a legume that grows very fast in summer, survives southern winters, and climbs by wrapping tendrils around supports, overwhelming trees, fences and barns.

segments.title: Kudzu taproots and root crowns
segments.summary: The hosts explain the huge taproot that stores energy and the root crowns that form where vines touch the ground, which makes kudzu hard to remove.

segments.title: Kudzu as food and medicine in Asia
segments.summary: Kudzu has long been used in traditional Chinese and Japanese medicine and as a starch thickener in foods such as mochi and noodles.

segments.title: Philadelphia Centennial and ornamental kudzu
segments.summary: The hosts say the popular story that kudzu was introduced at the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial Exposition is false, since the plants were destroyed. Kudzu was later sold as an ornamental vine on trellises, and it only became invasive when grown as ground cover.

segments.title: 1930s soil erosion and nitrogen fixing
segments.summary: Kudzu was promoted as a fix for eroded Southern soil during the 1930s, when the Soil Erosion Service (later the Soil Conservation Service) endorsed it. The hosts explain how plants fix nitrogen into the soil.

segments.title: Government planting programs
segments.summary: The government paid farmers about eight dollars an acre to plant kudzu, and the Civilian Conservation Corps and railroads planted it along roadways and tracks to stop erosion. By the mid-1940s about three million acres were planted on Southern farms.

segments.title: Break before Channing Cope segment
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before explaining who Channing Cope was.

segments.title: Channing Cope and kudzu boosterism
segments.summary: Channing Cope, a farm editor for the Atlanta Constitution with a popular radio show and column, promoted kudzu heavily and founded the Kudzu Club of America. About ten years later farmers reported cattle sickness and overrun farms, and the kudzu legend began to grow.

segments.title: Federal noxious weed listing and biodiversity
segments.summary: The USDA moved from calling kudzu not an improved cover crop in 1953 to listing it as a federal noxious weed in 1997. The hosts explain how the South's biodiversity, shaped by the glacial retreat, is threatened by invasive plants.

segments.title: Nitrogen pollution claims and kudzu study
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a 2010 study claiming kudzu adds air-polluting nitrogen compounds and a 2023 study finding that kudzu along roads traps car emissions. They note the hosts' own Southern pride in kudzu and joke about kudzu-dyed shirts and Confederate-era bumper stickers.

segments.title: Kudzu bug stink bug
segments.summary: The kudzu bug is a Japanese stink bug first spotted in the United States in 2009. It eats kudzu and can kill mature stands, but it is a nuisance pest that invades homes and stains clothes.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break and preview whether kudzu is overblown.

segments.title: Is kudzu overblown? Acreage statistics
segments.summary: The seven million acres figure often cited for kudzu in the South came from unreliable sources such as a garden club guide and a craft book. The US Forest Service counts about 227,000 acres in forests, and the hosts suggest that kudzu's visibility along highways creates selection bias.

segments.title: Other invasive plants in Alabama
segments.summary: The hosts compare kudzu with Chinese privet and Japanese honeysuckle, which cover more acreage in Alabama, and note that the true kudzu acreage is uncertain.

segments.title: Managing kudzu and ivy at home
segments.summary: Hosts describe kudzu on a garden island, English ivy on a privacy fence, and their own method of cutting vines and painting them with Crossbow herbicide.

segments.title: Mowing and digging out kudzu
segments.summary: Repeated mowing weakens kudzu by cutting off its leaves, and digging up the shallow root crowns kills the plant even though the large tuber remains. The hosts also discuss their discomfort with chefs using kudzu in cooking.

segments.title: Kudzu in culture: R.E.M. and Athens
segments.summary: Kudzu appears in poetry and music. The cover of R.E.M.'s album Murmur shows a kudzu-covered train trestle near Athens, which was taken down in 2020 and replaced in 2023 by a replica that is now part of the Firefly Trail.

segments.title: James Dickey poem Kudzu
segments.summary: Josh reads James Dickey's 1963 New Yorker poem Kudzu, and the hosts joke about adding music to it.

segments.title: Listener mail: Brooklyn Nine-Nine follow-up
segments.summary: Listener Victor writes to point out that Andy Samberg had a cameo in Brooklyn Nine-Nine, and shares a link and praise for the show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener, invite email at stuff podcast at iHeartRadio dot com, and sign off.
